newsitem.title: UK: Dry spell, late chill mark Europe's springtime.
newsitem.headline: Dry spell, late chill mark Europe's springtime.

text.p: Early wheat is said to be yellowing in parched fields in eastern England even as late frost threatens sugar beet in Serbia.
Europeans are puzzling about their weather, where spring has been marked by a prolonged dry spell in the West and bitter cold in the East.
Nothing so dramatic as the Red River floods in North Dakota has occurred in Europe and climatologists are wary of seeing any aberration.

"It is very difficult to draw a conclusion on whether there is any long term change from any one day or month or season," said Dr Goeff Jenkins of the Hadley Centre for Climate Prediction and Research.
"You have to draw a picture from the long term. The first indications of the effects of global warming are there, but you have to look at a couple of decades," he said.
But he added: "It's certainly been an unusual few months."
The impact is most directly felt by farmers who report real signs of damage to cereals in Britain and Spain.
Spain had its first rain for three months last week. Even so, its cereal crop could fall 15 percent, traders and farm experts said on Monday.
"Damage that has been done before the rain arrived can't be recovered now," one said.

Rain started in Spain last Thursday and continued over the weekend, although the effect on parched crops in the south has been minimal. The dry weather followed floods that reduced the amount of land sown.
"The rain's done us good but it's arrived too late," Jose Vazquez, spokesman for farmers' association ASAJA, told Reuters.
"This year has not been typical. First we had floods and then we had the driest March in the century," Vazquez said.

In Britain there is the perverse combination of a shortage of moisture and rain. Although there have frequently been grey skies in recent days and there have been some showers over the past week, with more forecast, there is no sign of the substantial rain that crops need.
French weather forecasters, officials and farmers have so far to refused to talk of a full blown drought, despite irrigation bans in some areas after a prolonged dry spell.

Environment Minister Corinne Lepage said last week the situation was worrying but not alarming. Rainfall has been as much as 50 percent below normal since January in the north of France and even lower in the south, triggering early forest fires.
France's bread basket Beauce region has received only 90 millimetres of rain this year, half of what normally falls.
Experts said that underground water tables were very low in the north, the centre, west and southwest but reservoirs were full.

"In the west, centre and in the north, the situation is not dramatic. If it rains in April the plants will not have suffered much," the analyst Strategie Grains said last week. But in the southeast drought has now done irreversible damage to the crops.

Farther to the east, conditions are better. German grain regions expect rain and milder temperatures in the second half of this week after a dry spell ,an official of the German weather service, DWD, said.
Soils had hardened under dry winds, and this slowed growth of the crops after a good start was made in March, he said.
"But the 1997 grain crop has never been threatened and hopefully there will be beneficial rain on its way very shortly," he said.

Growing conditions for Russia's winter grain crop were ideal in many regions this season, and early forecasts for the summer suggest good conditions will continue on the whole, said Viktor Trenin, head of the State Meteorological Service, last week.
He said estimates for winter kill losses in 1997 were eight to 10 percent below normal levels, although actual losses would not be known until the end of May.
In Siberia, however, where temperatures have been very high during the latter part of March and in early April, cold air over the coming weeks could lead to some crop damage.
Ukraine has had continuous rain recently, slowing planting of spring grains, but after a cooler, wet start, forecasters expect more sun and warmth in the second half of this week.
Overall the wet is good for the grain harvest, they said. But sugar beet planting has been delayed by the wet weather.

In the Balkans, Serbia's producers fear more frost could be a real disaster for the sugar beet crop. "Low temperatures in the past weeks have already destroyed newly emerging plants on 10,000 hectares," Milan Panic of the sugar producers' association Jugosecer said.
Heavy rain and snows in Romania have affected 18,000 hectares of wheat and barley, the agriculture ministry said.
